strategy_title: Develop a rigorous framework for measuring AI agent reliability
strategy_text: Investigate how autonomous and semi-autonomous AI agents can be measured objectively, reproducibly, and meaningfully across diverse tasks and operating conditions. Build an evaluation framework that distinguishes superficial task completion from correctness, robustness, and dependable behavior. Audit representative agent benchmarks for task-selection effects, environmental variability, evaluator bias, contamination, and weak completion oracles. Define operational measures for end-to-end success, partial completion, error severity, recovery, repeat-trial consistency, tool-use correctness, and resources per successful outcome. Specify how to evaluate stochastic agents, long dependency chains, long-running tasks, external tools, and changing environments. Propose repeated-trial protocols, uncertainty intervals, failure-distribution reporting, and comparisons under controlled compute, time, tool, and monetary budgets. State the evidence and replication needed for defensible reliability claims; separate benchmark-specific gains from general improvements. Deliver a protocol with task strata, outcome rubrics, baseline comparisons, statistical analysis, and explicit limits on what its results can establish.

strategy_runs.strategy_title: Understand failure propagation and recovery in autonomous AI agents
strategy_runs.strategy_text: Map how agents fail during extended, multi-step tasks and determine which failures are detectable, recoverable, or silently corrupt later results. Examine incorrect reasoning and plans, tool misuse, incomplete observations, stale or compressed context, instruction misunderstandings, environmental changes, and accumulated state errors. Trace concrete failure chains from initiating fault through subsequent actions to user-visible consequences; distinguish model limitations from architecture, orchestration, memory, interface, and environment failures. Investigate detection of silent errors, calibrated uncertainty versus actual failure, retry and replanning policies, escalation, and safe termination. Analyze checkpointing, state reconstruction, independent verification, rollback, idempotency, and human intervention as recovery mechanisms. For each mechanism, specify assumptions, failure modes, and measurable recovery criteria; compare recovery against restarting and continuing without intervention. Develop fault-injection scenarios and trace-based analyses that reveal propagation and test whether recovery restores correct state rather than merely producing a plausible answer. Deliver a failure taxonomy, causal workflow maps, and a prioritized set of falsifiable experiments, distinguishing observed evidence from proposed mechanisms.

reasoning_steps.title: 2. Preserve the core theorem with its original scope
reasoning_steps.argument: No change is needed to cycle 1, steps 1–3: in observationally identical W0 and W1, hidden-state-independent policy randomness gives the same probability q of issuing a first retry. When every issued retry commits before H and effects are irreversible, W0 success implies retry and W1 success implies no retry, so their success probabilities are bounded by q and 1-q. The worst-case failure bound of at least 1/2 consequently remains conditional on those premises. Without assured delivery, let N_i count additional committed effects by H in W_i. External-state correctness is exactly the event N_0=1 in W0 and N_1=0 in W1. No equality of the laws of N_0 and N_1 follows merely from identical information before the first retry. reasoning_steps.title: 3. Define the crash model and outcomes for the table
reasoning_steps.argument: Analyze one logical operation with fixed payload x. For a key k, write (c_k,r_k), where c_k is its number of irreversible committed effects and r_k is 1 iff a durable purported completion receipt exists. Let C=sum_k c_k count effects for the logical operation across all its keys. Initially all counts and receipt bits are zero. Attempts are serialized, including checking receipts, so the examples require no concurrency race. A receipt hit returns the stored receipt without performing another effect. A crash preserves completed durable transitions but discards the unfinished continuation; there is no background repair worker, separate effect-status query, or compensation. Stable recovery reuses the durably saved key and payload; regenerated recovery uses a previously unused key for the same logical operation. Keys do not collide, records do not expire, and payload mismatches are rejected. External-state correctness at H means C(H)=1. Full completion also requires a truthful terminal report. Eventual exactly-one completion means that after some finite time C remains one and truthful completion is reported, not merely that C transiently passes through one.

reasoning_steps.title: 4. Enumerate durable crash-boundary states
reasoning_steps.argument:
The following is an analytical transition table for a first, previously unseen key. A crash can occur at any displayed state; an atomic transition has no durable interior state.

| Implementation | Durable path on a receipt miss | Crash before first transition | Crash between transitions | Crash after both writes but before acknowledgment |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Atomic effect plus receipt | (0,0) -> (1,1) | (0,0) | Impossible under the contract | (1,1) |
| Effect before receipt | (0,0) -> (1,0) -> (1,1) | (0,0) | (1,0): effect exists, receipt absent | (1,1) |
| Receipt before effect | (0,0) -> (0,1) -> (1,1) | (0,0) | (0,1): receipt exists, effect absent | (1,1) |

A crash after acknowledgment but before the client durably saves completion leaves the same service states as the final column. In the receipt-before-effect row, 'receipt' deliberately denotes a record treated by this implementation as completed; an explicitly pending record with an independently correct recovery protocol is a different implementation. When effect and receipt involve different downstream systems, the atomic row applies only if the stipulated atomicity actually covers the external effect.

reasoning_steps.title: 5. Cross implementation with recovery-key policy
reasoning_steps.argument:
In this six-case table, 'clean retry' means a delivered retry that runs without another crash and whose response is delivered. Traces use the durable states from step 4; they are constructed possibilities, not observations.

| Service / key policy | Before either write | Interior crash boundary | After effect and receipt, acknowledgment lost | Consequence under continued recovery |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Atomic / stable | (0,0); retry k commits (1,1) | No such durable boundary | (1,1); retry k returns receipt, C stays 1 | At-most-one invariant always; a clean retry resolves either surviving state |
| Atomic / regenerated | Fresh k' can cleanly create the first effect if the old attempt never committed | No such durable boundary | k has (1,1); retry k' commits (1,1), so C=2 | Per-key uniqueness survives, logical-operation uniqueness does not |
| Effect-before-receipt / stable | Retry k can complete normally | k=(1,0); retry misses receipt, performs another effect, then writes receipt: (2,1) | k=(1,1); retry returns receipt without another effect | One gap crash followed by a clean retry duplicates; later progress does not remove it |
| Effect-before-receipt / regenerated | Fresh k' can complete normally if no old effect exists | k=(1,0); clean retry k' creates another effect, so C=2 | k=(1,1); clean retry k' again makes C=2 | A fresh key bypasses both recorded and unrecorded prior effects |
| Receipt-before-effect / stable | Retry k can complete normally | k=(0,1); every retry returns the receipt, so C remains 0 | k=(1,1); retry returns receipt with C=1 | Gap crash causes permanent omission under this handler, even with perfect subsequent delivery |
| Receipt-before-effect / regenerated | Fresh k' can complete normally | k=(0,1); clean fresh-key retry can create one effect and repair this particular omission | k=(1,1); clean retry k' creates a second effect | Fresh keys repair one constructed gap history but duplicate the post-effect history; no general exactly-one guarantee |

For every row, if the first attempt crashes before any write and all further useful execution is delayed past H, C(H)=0. That is a deadline omission even in the atomic/stable case, not a violation of its at-most-one safety invariant.

reasoning_steps.title: 6. Prove the atomic/stable invariant and its liveness boundary
reasoning_steps.argument: For atomic/stable recovery, induction over serialized service transitions proves (c_k,r_k) is always either (0,0) or (1,1). The base case is (0,0). A receipt miss makes the single atomic transition to (1,1); a receipt hit leaves that state unchanged; a crash preserves one of those states. All attempts use k, so C=c_k<=1. Thus a receipt cannot falsely certify a missing effect, and a lost acknowledgment cannot cause duplication. If recovery eventually has a surviving delivered call and returns its response, that call either creates the unique effect or retrieves its existing receipt, establishing eventual effect-and-receipt completion. A client that then persists completion and reports truthfully can finish. Infinite crashes, permanently lost responses, or exhausted retry budgets defeat that liveness premise without defeating the safety invariant.

reasoning_steps.title: 7. Explain why weaker invariants fail
reasoning_steps.argument: Atomic recording with fresh keys proves c_k<=1 separately for each k, but it does not bound sum_k c_k by one. Effect-before-receipt lacks the implication 'effect exists => receipt exists'; the gap permits an already committed action to be re-executed. Receipt-before-effect lacks the reverse implication 'receipt exists => effect exists'; the gap suppresses work that never happened and can produce a false completion report. These are distinct failure-propagation paths: ambiguity -> retry -> duplication versus premature certification -> suppressed retry -> omission. A receipt-before-effect intent log with a correct pending/completed distinction and reconciliation is outside the table's suppress-on-hit semantics, not refuted by this local omission trace. Likewise, effect-side deduplication would change the effect-before-receipt model.

reasoning_steps.title: 8. Separate eventual progress, deadline completion, and delayed duplication
reasoning_steps.argument: Eventual successful delivery supplies no fixed-H guarantee: an otherwise successful execution can have its first useful call or response delayed until H+1. As one sufficient stronger condition for atomic/stable recovery, suppose recovery starts at t0, faults cease by t0+B, the next retry is sent within delta, its full service interaction and response take at most S, and durable client completion plus truthful reporting take at most A. If t0+B+delta+S+A<=H, completion by H follows from step 6. These are hard conditional bounds, not measured latencies. For the other five cases, finite faults followed by clean progress still admit the table's persistent omission or duplication traces; progress alone cannot repair their safety/certification defects. Moreover C(H)=1 is only a horizon-specific count: a regenerated-key retry after H can create delayed duplication. A deadline experiment must separately specify whether outstanding or future actions are canceled and audit a later settlement horizon. Atomic/stable safety covers later same-key retries as long as retention and key identity persist.

reasoning_steps.title: 9. Specify the next discriminating test and retain evidential limits

Inject a single crash before the first write, in each available interior gap, and after both writes with the acknowledgment withheld; separately crash the client before completion persistence. Follow with a clean retry, then repeat under permanent outage, delayed response beyond H, and an additional late retry. Audit C at H and a prespecified settlement horizon, receipt truth, client reports, recovery calls, latency, and cost. Include no-fault controls and matched payloads, retry schedules, budgets, and H across arms; retain every attempted run. Deterministic boundary coverage should precede seeded stochastic schedules and independent task-cluster repetitions. Discriminators are C=2 for effect-before-receipt/stable and post-commit regenerated-key traces, C=0 with a receipt for receipt-before-effect/stable, and only (0,0)/(1,1) for atomic/stable. An apparent contradiction requires inspecting the actual semantics and injection location rather than treating finite agreement as proof. This refines the unresolved execution obligation but does not discharge it.

The transition table concerns one fixed-payload logical operation with irreversible effects, initially empty durable receipt state, and serialized attempts; each individual completed write survives a crash.

A receipt hit suppresses further effects and returns a purported completion receipt. Crashes discard unfinished continuations, with no independent reconciliation, compensation, or effect-status lookup.

Stable recovery preserves a durable pre-send key and payload. Regenerated recovery uses a fresh key for the same operation. Keys are collision-free, records persist, and payload mismatches are rejected.
The atomic implementation serializes receipt checks and commits the actual external effect and durable receipt together, not merely a local intention to cause a downstream effect.

Eventual full completion is conditional on a surviving delivered service call, service progress, eventual response delivery, and client persistence and truthful reporting. Completion by H additionally requires the stated timing bounds.

strategy_runs.strategy_title: Test architectural mechanisms for dependable agent outcomes
strategy_runs.strategy_text: Compare architectural interventions intended to improve agent reliability, including constrained tool interfaces, typed action and observation schemas, explicit state and provenance, planning and execution separation, checkpoints, bounded retries, independent verification, uncertainty-triggered escalation, sandboxing, and safe stopping. Select representative multi-step tasks and controlled perturbations involving tool errors, partial observations, stale data, environment changes, and ambiguous instructions. Establish a transparent baseline and change one mechanism at a time before testing justified combinations. Measure verified task success, severity-weighted errors, silent failures, recovery rate, consistency, latency, token/tool use, and cost per verified success. Use repeated trials and report uncertainty; control model version, prompts, tools, budgets, task difficulty, and environment wherever feasible. Test whether gains persist on held-out tasks and under distribution shifts, and whether interventions introduce new failure modes or merely shift costs. Separate implemented and empirically evaluated mechanisms from conceptual proposals; do not infer causal benefit from correlations or a single benchmark. Deliver an evidence table linking each mechanism to its assumptions, measured effects, costs, regressions, and unresolved validation needs.

pending_investigation.claim: Under the explicit ledger contract below, atomic, durable idempotency prevents more than one committed transfer for the same scoped key, including concurrent retries, acknowledgment loss, and crash recovery. If every attempt for one intended operation uses that key, this gives at-most-one commitment for that operation—not guaranteed completion, correct authorization, timely settlement, or end-to-end task success. The specification and paired oracle truth table below distinguish those properties. This is an analytical specification, not an executed experiment or measured architectural benefit.
pending_investigation.method: Specify a small ledger, client retry policy, independent outcome oracle, and deterministic paired fault schedules. Hypothesis for a future experiment: stable-key atomic deduplication reduces duplicate commitments after ambiguous timeouts without unacceptable omission, latency, or cost regressions. The discriminating analytical case is a committed request whose acknowledgment is lost: baseline retries can commit twice, whereas the specified intervention replays one durable receipt. Negative controls include dropped requests, missed receipt deadlines, and unauthorized requests; contract-breaking controls include regenerated keys, early record deletion, and non-atomic effect/record writes. Both arms must use isolated identical snapshots, identical authorization and settlement rules, fixed model/prompt versions and resource ceilings, and the same retry policy; baseline ignores the otherwise identical key field. Safeguard overhead counts against the intervention budget. No runtime is available, so no program or execution is requested. The current action addresses the specification portion of the unresolved ledger/oracle obligation; implementation, audit, inference calibration, and empirical effectiveness remain open.

reasoning_steps.title: 1. Scope, economic effect, and authorization
reasoning_steps.argument: One task intends one transfer p*=(run, operation, source, recipient, positive integer amount, currency). Integer minor units avoid rounding ambiguity. A trusted fixture issues a grant g binding the principal, exact p*, and commit-valid interval [0,E]. The expected intent comes from this fixture, not from an agent-supplied label. Authorization is checked at the commitment linearization point, including revocation, account ownership, and sufficient funds. A grant permits repeated matching submissions during its interval; it is deliberately not a one-use token. Otherwise a one-use authorization service would itself supply the duplicate-prevention intervention. The fixture permits no grant renewal. Commitment atomically posts balanced debit/credit entries; settlement subsequently marks that same transaction final and never posts another debit. This is a closed ledger, not an unmodeled external payment rail.

reasoning_steps.title: 2. Minimal auditable state
reasoning_steps.argument: The state is (balances, grants/revocations, transaction log L, deduplication map D, request queue, response queue, client journal). Each transaction contains a unique txid, exact payload, grant identity/version, authorization result, commit sequence/time, and status COMMITTED or SETTLED. D maps a scoped key K to the complete payload and durable committed receipt. Requests have distinct attempt IDs but share an operation identity. Their lifecycle is SENT -> DROPPED or QUEUED -> REJECTED, REPLAYED, or COMMITTED. Responses separately become DELIVERED, DELAYED, or LOST. Client journal entries record the intended payload/key before sending, attempt counts, observed receipts, and final output. Authoritative server events record validation, commitment, replay/conflict, recovery, and settlement; transport fault events record drops and delays. Economic events and their deduplication records must survive the same crashes. The oracle reads server state and the fault schedule, not merely the client's journal.

reasoning_steps.title: 3. Key scope, binding, and lifetime
reasoning_steps.argument: Define K=(isolated-run epoch, tenant, authenticated principal, transfer-endpoint version, opaque key). One intended operation receives one key, durably journaled before its first send and reused after every timeout or client restart. Distinct operations require distinct keys. D binds K to exact canonical payload equality, including operation ID and all economic fields; equality is not inferred solely from an unchecked hash. Reuse with a different payload returns KEY_CONFLICT and performs no write. Lookup and receipt replay require current read authorization; possession of a key is not authentication. Records survive restart, failover, and snapshot recovery and have no TTL while the namespace exists. Namespace disposal is allowed only with permanent rejection of its old epochs, including restored replicas. A production retention interval would instead need a justified upper bound on every possible replay and restore path; the agent retry deadline alone is insufficient.

reasoning_steps.title: 4. Atomic server transition and its baseline
reasoning_steps.argument: For intervention A, Execute(K,p,g) first authenticates access. In one serializable durable transaction: if D[K] exists with p, return its recorded receipt without an economic write; if it exists with a different payload, reject; otherwise recheck current authorization, commit-valid time, and funds, then atomically append one balanced transaction and insert D[K]=(p,receipt). A crash exposes either both writes or neither. Concurrent requests linearize through this transaction; there is no independently durable 'key reserved, effect unfinished' state. Rejected attempts do not reserve keys or cache negative results. A receipt replay may occur after grant expiry or revocation if read access remains valid, but cannot create a new transfer. Baseline B performs the same fresh authorization and balanced posting for each executed attempt, ignoring D. In both arms acknowledgment generation follows durable commitment; losing an acknowledgment never rolls back commitment. Settlement is an idempotent txid-based status transition held fixed between arms.

reasoning_steps.title: 5. Bounded retry, delayed responses, and settlement closure
reasoning_steps.argument: Fix an agent deadline D_agent, grant expiry E>D_agent, maximum retries R, timeout/backoff schedule, and total call/time/token/monetary ceilings. At most R+1 write attempts may be sent, all before D_agent; reads and reconciliation also consume prespecified budgets. Timeouts mean UNKNOWN, not FAILED or CANCELED. A delayed original request may execute after a retry or after client stopping. A matching committed receipt delivered before D_agent permits final output; subsequent responses cannot trigger a new operation or reset the retry count. A delayed response alone never changes ledger state. At exhaustion the client outputs UNKNOWN/ESCALATE, not success. Choose settlement horizon H>E+s, where each committed transaction settles within s in the core contract. At H, Q=1 means all run transactions are settled and every queued or future old-grant request is permanently unable to create another economic effect. Commit-time expiry supplies this fence; a client stop does not. Fault tests may violate settlement progress, in which case Q can be zero.

reasoning_steps.title: 6. Exact success, harmful-event, and safe-stop predicates
reasoning_steps.argument: Let L_H be all run-attributable economic commitments through H, including requests still executing after the client stops. Order them by authoritative commit sequence. A commitment is bad if it differs from fixture intent p*, was unauthorized at commitment, or is the second or later commitment for that one intended operation. A settlement event is bad if it settles a bad commitment or creates any extra economic posting. Let Harm_H indicate any bad commitment or settlement by H, and DelayedHarm_(D_agent,H] indicate any such bad event whose event time is in (D_agent,H]. Thus a correct first commitment after D_agent misses the deadline but is not automatically harm; a duplicate committed before D_agent and settled afterward is delayed harm under this event-based definition. Exact task success Y_H=1 iff: L_H contains exactly one commitment, it equals p* and was authorized, its commit time is at most D_agent, it is settled by H, no bad settlement occurred, Q=1, the client output by D_agent contains its matching txid/payload/committed receipt, and all client budget limits were respected. Otherwise Y_H=0. A safe omission stop requires an UNKNOWN/ESCALATE output, L_H empty, Q=1, and no harmful event; it is not task success. Missing audit data produce UNKNOWN labels, not invented zero harm or known success. These are horizon-specific predicates, not claims of lifetime safety.

reasoning_steps.title: 7. Proof of the duplicate-commit exclusion
reasoning_steps.argument: Initially fix any K with D[K] absent. Induct over serialized server transitions. A rejection, replay, response event, or settlement creates no commitment. The first successful fresh execution inserts exactly one commitment and D[K] together. Thereafter every matching execution takes the replay branch and every mismatching execution takes the conflict branch. Crash recovery preserves both the commitment and D[K], so it cannot restore the absent-key state while retaining the effect. Therefore the commitment count for K is at most one for every finite history. Serialization handles simultaneous attempts; transport order and lost acknowledgments are irrelevant to this invariant. If K is initially occupied, no fresh commitment is possible under it. If every attempt for one operation uses the same K, that operation inherits the bound. A stable operation label without stable K does not establish the premise.

reasoning_steps.title: 8. What the invariant does not prove
reasoning_steps.argument: Zero commitments satisfies at-most-one. All requests can be dropped, authorization can expire, funds can be insufficient, a receipt can arrive too late, or settlement can fail. Conditional completion additionally follows only if an authorized matching execution linearizes before D_agent, its receipt is delivered and correctly output before D_agent within budget, settlement and closure hold by H, and no other faulty path changes the ledger. Then the invariant supplies uniqueness and these additional conditions supply every remaining clause of Y_H. This is not an eventual-delivery guarantee under bounded retries. Wrong fixture intent, a compromised authorizer, a separate non-deduplicated downstream effect, and writes under fresh keys remain outside the invariant. Atomic idempotency also does not undo a first incorrect authorized transfer.

reasoning_steps.title: 9. Concrete paired trace conventions
reasoning_steps.argument: For the truth table use D_agent=10, E=12, H=15, s<=2, R=1, sends at times 0 and, if no valid receipt has arrived, 4; the timeout occurs at 3. Accounts contain enough funds for both baseline attempts. Ordinary commitments occur at 1 or 5, settle one unit later, and delivered receipts arrive before 10 unless specified. Both arms receive the same attempt-indexed fault schedule and isolated initial state. A replay produces no settlement event because it creates no transaction. The tuple is (n_D,n_H,r,q,y,d): commitment counts by 10 and 15, whether a matching receipt was output by 10, closure Q, success Y_H, and DelayedHarm_(10,15]. A valid local receipt does not certify uniqueness: r may be 1 when y is 0. All entries are deductions from specified traces, not observations. The table is a set of discriminating witnesses, not exhaustive state-space verification.

reasoning_steps.title: 12. Key collision and recovery introduce different risks
reasoning_steps.argument: A separate two-operation regression test is necessary because the primary task requires only one operation. Give two valid grants for distinct operations p1 and p2, sufficient funds, timely receipts, and settlement. With distinct keys both arms have per-operation counts (1,1) and satisfy the two-operation rubric. If the client incorrectly assigns the same K to both, B still obtains (1,1), whereas correct A obtains (1,0): p2 is rejected as KEY_CONFLICT because operation identity is part of the payload. A's two-operation success is false, but duplicate/unauthorized harm is zero. If payload checking instead omits operation identity and silently returns p1's receipt for p2, that is an additional implementation defect; an oracle checking operation IDs rejects it. Conversely, changing K to escape a conflict after an ambiguous first commitment can create two effects for the first operation. Conflicts therefore require reconciliation or explicit escalation, not automatic new-key retry. Deduplication introduces storage, contention, access-control, retention, and reconciliation obligations; these can shift risk from duplication to omission or availability.

strategy_snapshot.title: Develop a rigorous framework for measuring AI agent reliability
Understand failure propagation and recovery in autonomous AI agents
Test architectural mechanisms for dependable agent outcomes

problem:
Autonomous AI agents are increasingly expected to complete complex tasks involving planning, reasoning, external tools, persistent state, and interaction with changing environments. Demonstrations and benchmark results show that agents can perform many such tasks, but provide limited evidence that they remain dependable across repeated executions, unfamiliar conditions, long-running workflows, and settings where mistakes have significant consequences. This project asks how autonomous and semi-autonomous agents can be evaluated and engineered to deliver reliable, correct, recoverable, and reproducible results across extended, multi-step tasks.

Agent reliability is a system-level property. Probabilistic decisions, dynamically constructed plans, incomplete observations, tool interfaces, memory, orchestration, and external state all affect whether the intended outcome is actually achieved. Small errors can propagate through later actions and yield plausible but incorrect results. An agent may claim completion without satisfying the task, recover from one failure while introducing another, or behave differently across otherwise comparable runs. Reliability therefore cannot be inferred from fluent explanations, a single successful trajectory, agreement among similar models, or benchmark scores alone.

Investigate three connected questions. First, how should reliability be defined and measured so evaluation reflects actual correctness, robustness, consistency, recoverability, tool-use quality, and cost rather than superficial completion? Second, what are the principal sources of failure, how do errors propagate through multi-step execution, and which signals and interventions can detect, contain, or recover from failures without creating additional risks? Third, which engineering mechanisms demonstrably improve outcomes, and how can their effects be established through controlled experiments rather than architectural intuition or anecdotal success? The strategies approach these questions from complementary measurement, failure-analysis, and intervention perspectives; none presumes a preferred architecture.

Use available research literature, software-reliability principles, empirical evaluation methods, and documented agent-system designs. Examine the relationship between model capability and end-to-end system reliability, including tool interfaces, state management, verification, orchestration, uncertainty handling, changing environments, recovery, and execution budgets. Assess benchmark sensitivity to task selection, evaluator bias, contamination, and weak completion oracles. Consider stochastic behavior, repeated trials, long dependency chains, held-out tasks, fault injection, independent correctness judgments, and uncertainty in estimated success rates. Where comparisons are proposed, make assumptions and controls explicit, including model and prompt versions, task difficulty, environment, tool access, compute, latency, and monetary budgets.

Evaluate competing approaches on the strength and limits of their evidence. Distinguish measured results from formal or theoretical arguments, proposed mechanisms, and unsupported claims; do not present planned experiments as completed or infer causal benefit from correlation. Account for correlated errors among agents or critics that share models and training data, and for the difficulty of constructing an independent oracle for open-ended tasks. Analyze tradeoffs among reliability, flexibility, recovery overhead, latency, and computational expense, including cases where a safeguard shifts rather than removes risk.

The intended outcome is an evidence-grounded account of what reliability claims current evaluations can support, a practical and reproducible evaluation framework, a causal taxonomy of important failure and recovery modes, and architectural principles whose limits are explicit. Identify unresolved questions and specify discriminating experiments needed to validate competing claims. The project is open-ended: conclusions should remain proportional to the quality, independence, and generality of available evidence.

output.claim: A stratified, paired comparison can certify a positive reliability difference without assuming independent judge errors or independent repeated runs. For each stratum h, let C_A indicate joint automated/reference acceptance of system A, and D_B indicate joint automated/reference rejection of baseline B. Assume Pr(C_A=1,Y_A=0|h)≤η_Ah and Pr(D_B=1,Y_B=1|h)≤η_Bh, where Y denotes actual success. With fixed population weights w_h, n_h independent paired task clusters per stratum, arbitrary dependence within clusters, and the cluster score Z_hi equal to the mean of C_A+D_B−1 over scheduled run pairs, define S=Σ_h w_h²/n_h and E=Σ_h w_h(η_Ah+η_Bh). Then L=max{−1, Σ_h w_h mean_i(Z_hi)−E−sqrt[2S log(1/α)]} is a one-sided (1−α) lower confidence bound on p_A−p_B. Conservative missing-data scores may replace Z_hi as specified below. Thus L>0 supports improvement only for the fixed target distribution, protocol, budgets, and truth-error allowances.
output.method: Develop a standalone conditional lemma addressing the ledger's stratification, paired-comparison, and missingness obligations. The hypothesis is that improvement certification requires a lower bound for A and an upper bound for B, not two lower bounds. The discriminating analytical outcomes are an explicit baseline false-rejection allowance, a cluster-level weighted confidence bound, and a counterexample to subtracting lower bounds. The supplied extract of artifact 0310e2ff-4aa0-4c95-b1a8-795559e484b8 motivates the extension, but the argument is rederived here rather than treating its prior assertions as certified premises. Its original and the pointer-only historical artifact df5067f1-d298-4203-a108-a2e7056af576 are unavailable for inspection. The relevant recorded provider failure 4ffc6be5-d3a7-4505-bf62-8b62516e2d2e supplies no mathematical evidence; this response takes a bounded analytical action rather than repeating an operational request. Both computation runtimes are unavailable, so no coverage experiment is claimed. A proposed next test is a finite-support repeated-panel coverage experiment with known truth, dependent run pairs, correlated judges, and adversarial missingness.

reasoning_steps.title: 1. Define the target population and paired sampling unit
reasoning_steps.argument: Fix H task strata, distributions D_h, weights w_h≥0 summing to one, positive integer cluster counts n_h for positive-weight strata, and positive integer run counts r_h. For system s∈{A,B}, define p_sh as the probability of actual rubric satisfaction when a task is drawn from D_h and a run is selected uniformly from its scheduled r_h-run batch. The target contrast is Δ=Σ_h w_h(p_Ah−p_Bh). Each cluster contains both systems' batches on the same sampled task. Clusters are independent across all h,i and identically distributed within each stratum. Dependence among all runs, systems, and judges inside a cluster is unrestricted.

reasoning_steps.title: 2. Fix controls and prevent interference
reasoning_steps.argument: Fix versions, prompts, success rubrics, observation horizons, tools, retry policies, and compute/time/monetary caps before outcomes. Evaluate both systems from equivalent isolated environment snapshots; randomize execution order where order could matter, without allowing one system to alter the other's state. Count safeguards, verification, and recovery against each system's stated execution budget. Equal caps define the primary budget-matched contrast; unequal budgets define a different contrast and must be labeled accordingly. Identical task distributions and isolated execution make the paired marginals match the target estimand. These are requirements for an implementation, not properties established for an actual benchmark.

reasoning_steps.title: 3. State directional truth-error allowances
reasoning_steps.argument: For each run, O_s∈{0,1} is automated acceptance, R_s∈{0,1} is reference certification, and Y_s∈{0,1} is actual success. Set C_A=1{O_A=1,R_A=1} and D_B=1{O_B=0,R_B=0}. Under uniform run selection within stratum h, assume e_Ah=Pr(C_A=1,Y_A=0|h)≤η_Ah and e_Bh=Pr(D_B=1,Y_B=1|h)≤η_Bh. These are unconditional error probabilities within the stratum, not conditional error rates among accepted or rejected cases. The second allowance is new relative to a one-system lower-bound construction: jointly rejected B executions can nevertheless be genuine successes. Neither allowance follows from agreement between the judges.

reasoning_steps.title: 4. Derive the population lower contrast
reasoning_steps.argument: Pointwise, Y_A≥C_A−C_A(1−Y_A). Also 1−Y_B≥D_B−D_BY_B, hence Y_B≤1−D_B+D_BY_B. Subtracting and taking stratum expectations gives p_Ah−p_Bh≥E[C_A+D_B−1|h]−e_Ah−e_Bh. Weighting and applying the allowances yields Δ≥μ−E, where μ=Σ_h w_h E[C_A+D_B−1|h] and E=Σ_h w_h(η_Ah+η_Bh). No independence of truth, automated judgments, reference judgments, or the two systems is used in these inequalities.

reasoning_steps.title: 5. Explain the baseline upper-bound requirement
reasoning_steps.argument: The same derivation gives p_Bh≤min{1,1−Pr(D_B=1|h)+η_Bh}. A restriction only on jointly accepted failures leaves Y_B=1 everywhere observationally possible: that assignment creates no accepted failures. Consequently such a restriction alone supplies no nontrivial baseline upper bound. Likewise, p_A≥L_A and p_B≥L_B do not imply Δ≥L_A−L_B. For example, L_A=0.8, L_B=0.7, p_A=0.8, and p_B=1 satisfy both lower bounds, but Δ=−0.2 rather than the purported lower bound 0.1. This is an analytical counterexample, not a measured agent result.

reasoning_steps.title: 6. Reduce dependent runs to bounded cluster scores
reasoning_steps.argument: For task cluster i in stratum h, let Z_hi=(1/r_h)Σ_j(C_Ahij+D_Bhij−1). Every Z_hi lies in [−1,1], and E[Z_hi]=E[C_A+D_B−1|h] by the definition of uniform run selection. Thus μ̂=Σ_h(w_h/n_h)Σ_i Z_hi has expectation μ. Only the cluster scores need be independent. Increasing r_h does not increase the number of independent task units, and no factor r_h enters the worst-case concentration guarantee. Pairing may reduce actual variability, but this range-based bound does not assume or guarantee a variance reduction.

reasoning_steps.title: 7. Establish the finite-sample confidence guarantee
reasoning_steps.argument: For each independent weighted summand (w_h/n_h)Z_hi, the range length is 2w_h/n_h. The bounded-variable exponential-moment inequality gives E exp[λ(μ̂−μ)]≤exp(λ²S/2), with S=Σ_h w_h²/n_h. Markov's inequality followed by minimization over λ>0 yields Pr(μ̂−μ≥t)≤exp[−t²/(2S)]. Taking t=sqrt[2S log(1/α)] gives μ≥μ̂−t with probability at least 1−α. Combining with step 4 proves Δ≥μ̂−t−E on this event. Since Δ≥−1 always, clipping the lower endpoint at −1 preserves coverage. This is the standard bounded-sum concentration method applied to independent tasks, not run-level binomial analysis.

reasoning_steps.title: 8. Handle missing labels and scheduled attempts conservatively
reasoning_steps.argument: Retain a preregistered roster of all sampled task clusters and scheduled run slots; never divide only by completed runs. Record C_A as 1 only when both acceptance labels are available and equal 1, otherwise use 0. Record D_B as 1 only when both rejection labels are available and equal 0, otherwise use 0. These replacements are pointwise no larger than the corresponding complete-data indicators, so the resulting score Z̃_hi≤Z_hi. A wholly missing pair receives −1. Therefore μ̂_obs≤μ̂ for every realized missingness pattern, and the same lower confidence formula remains conservative, even when missingness depends on outcomes. For missing attempts this argument requires well-defined full scheduled-execution outcomes and no interference from omission with other clusters. A known protocol crash can instead be labeled directly according to the rubric. If omitted tasks cannot be enumerated, or cancellation changes other executions' distributions, this argument does not apply; the target population or design must be repaired.

reasoning_steps.title: 9. Allocate error across calibration, outcomes, and monitoring
reasoning_steps.argument: The stated 1−α guarantee treats η_Ah and η_Bh as valid fixed population bounds. If calibration instead supplies simultaneous upper allowances with failure probability at most β, the evaluation failure probability is at most α_eval+β by a union bound; independence between calibration and evaluation is unnecessary for this union bound, though each component guarantee still needs justification. For prespecified binary metrics k and deterministic analysis looks ℓ, allocate α_kℓ>0 with Σ_k,ℓ α_kℓ+β≤α_total and apply the theorem separately at each look using its fixed sample counts. A union bound then gives simultaneous coverage, permitting selection of a reporting or stopping look from that schedule. This does not justify unplanned metric selection, adaptive task sampling, changing protocols, or arbitrary continuous monitoring.

reasoning_steps.title: 10. Check boundary cases and interpretation
reasoning_steps.argument: With H=1 and r=1 the result reduces to a paired bounded-score comparison. Zero-weight strata contribute nothing; a positive-weight stratum with no sampled clusters cannot use the displayed formula and must instead receive its trivial contrast lower bound −1 or be sampled. If all observations are missing, every observed score is −1 and clipping returns −1, certifying nothing. With perfect judges C_A=Y_A and D_B=1−Y_B, both allowances can be zero and Z is the actual paired success difference. Under arbitrary within-task dependence, identical repeated runs do not tighten the radius. A positive endpoint supports a fixed-protocol success advantage, not automatically a causal architectural benefit or a safety guarantee.

reasoning_steps.title: 11. Specify a discriminating implementation test
reasoning_steps.argument: When execution is available, generate two-stratum finite-support task populations with exactly calculable Δ, e_Ah, and e_Bh. Vary n_h, r_h, stratum weights, within-task dependence from independent to identical runs, and shared judge errors. Include outcome-dependent label deletion while retaining every scheduled slot. Across independent panels, measure noncoverage of the stated endpoint and compare it with an intentionally naive run-independent analysis. Include violated-allowance and cross-cluster shared-state controls, which are outside the theorem. Report Monte Carlo uncertainty and endpoint width; finite coverage agreement tests implementation and these specified populations, not universal validity. This experiment has not been executed.

assumptions: The target strata, nonnegative population weights summing to one, sample counts, run counts, systems, budgets, rubrics, observation horizons, and execution policies are fixed before outcomes.

Paired task clusters are independent across strata and tasks, identically distributed within each stratum, and sampled from the stated target populations; arbitrary dependence is allowed within each cluster.
Systems execute under equivalent isolated conditions without cross-system or cross-cluster interference, and Y denotes actual rubric satisfaction.

For every positive-weight stratum, the target-population error probabilities Pr(C_A=1,Y_A=0|h) and Pr(D_B=1,Y_B=1|h) are bounded by the stated η_Ah and η_Bh. These allowances are not empirically established here.

All sampled clusters and scheduled slots are enumerated and retained. The missing-attempt extension requires well-defined full scheduled-execution outcomes and omissions that do not change other clusters' outcomes or target distributions.

For the main fixed-sample bound, n_h and r_h are positive integers in positive-weight strata and 0<α<1. Any calibration or simultaneous-monitoring extension must satisfy its separately stated error guarantees.

output.claim: Conditional impossibility result: after an ambiguous acknowledgment for a non-idempotent external action, an agent that cannot distinguish 'not committed' from 'committed' before deciding whether to retry cannot guarantee exactly one external effect using local checkpoint restoration, replanning, or restarting alone. For two such indistinguishable histories, every randomized recovery policy has worst-case probability of violating the exactly-once requirement at least 1/2. This identifies a concrete failure-propagation mechanism, not an observed agent failure rate.
output.method: Analyze a minimal external-write workflow using two constructed fault histories. Hypothesis: restoring an agent's local state is insufficient to restore consistency with external state when an acknowledgment is lost. The discriminating analytical outcome is an indistinguishability bound; the proposed empirical discriminator is a paired fault-injection test measuring actual external effects rather than completion claims. Assumptions are explicit below. Both execution runtimes are unavailable, so no experiment was dispatched. The supplied extract of artifact 0310e2ff-4aa0-4c95-b1a8-795559e484b8 was reviewed for scope: it concerns conditional correctness measurement, assumes independent task clusters, leaves reference validity and persistent-state outcomes unresolved, and contains no relevant completed computation. Its original is unavailable and its extract is incomplete. I adopt only the methodological caution that judge agreement does not establish external-state correctness; I do not transfer its reliability formulas or its next question to this recovery claim. The recorded cancellation and timeout motivate a compact standalone analytical result, not repetition of an unavailable failed request.

reasoning_steps.title: Define the workflow and recovery requirement
reasoning_steps.argument: A task requires exactly one irreversible external effect, such as appending one uniquely identifiable but non-deduplicated transaction to a write-only service. The agent records a local pending operation, sends it, and expects an acknowledgment. Let C be the number of committed effects for that logical operation. At a prespecified deadline H, success requires C=1 and a truthful terminal report. C=0 is incomplete; C>=2 is duplication. Safe escalation is recorded separately and is not successful completion. The impossibility argument uses only the necessary condition C=1, so adding report correctness cannot weaken it.

reasoning_steps.title: Construct two observationally identical histories
reasoning_steps.argument: In history W0, the original request is dropped before committing, leaving C=0. In W1, it commits once but its acknowledgment is lost, leaving C=1. A crash then restores the same local pending checkpoint in both histories. The service exposes no status query, durable deduplication, compensating operation, or other distinguishing observation before the first possible retry or deadline. Thus the local transcript and all information available for that decision are identical. This construction does not apply if an authoritative receipt or another informative observation is available.

reasoning_steps.title: Derive the randomized lower bound
reasoning_steps.argument: Let q be the probability that the policy issues at least one retry before H. Because the two histories are indistinguishable until that decision, q is the same in both. Assume every issued retry commits at least once before H, and committed effects cannot be removed. In W0, success requires a retry, so Pr(success|W0)<=q. In W1, any retry creates duplication, so Pr(success|W1)<=1-q. Therefore min{Pr(success|W0),Pr(success|W1)}<=min(q,1-q)<=1/2. Equivalently, worst-case failure probability is at least 1/2. Additional retries or false completion reports can only reduce success. Under an equal mixture of W0 and W1, average success is also at most 1/2. These are bounds for the constructed histories, not population estimates.

reasoning_steps.title: Check tightness, deterministic policies, and termination
reasoning_steps.argument: Within this construction, a fair coin that chooses between one retry and no retry achieves external-state correctness probability 1/2 in each history when the chosen retry commits exactly once. Thus the external-effect bound is tight, although truthful completion may require more information. A deterministic retry duplicates W1; a deterministic stop leaves W0 incomplete. Waiting forever does not satisfy the finite deadline. Safe stopping can guarantee no additional duplicate but cannot guarantee task completion. If retry delivery is not assured, the upper bounds still hold, but the tightness example need not.

reasoning_steps.title: Identify the propagation path and the boundary of local recovery
reasoning_steps.argument: The causal chain is ambiguous transport outcome -> divergent external state hidden behind the same local pending state -> retry duplicates an already committed effect, or stopping omits an uncommitted effect -> later workflow steps consume an incorrect effect count. Replaying the checkpoint, compressing memory differently, changing the plan, or replacing the model supplies no new information about which history occurred. Such changes therefore cannot evade the bound while the information and action assumptions remain unchanged. Rolling back local memory does not roll back the external effect. An independent status observation or a different service contract changes the assumptions and can change recoverability.

reasoning_steps.title: Give a sufficient service contract that changes the scope
reasoning_steps.argument: Suppose the agent durably stores a logical-operation key k and payload x before sending. The service maintains a durable record M[k] and atomically couples the external effect with installing its receipt in M[k]. A call with a new key performs the effect and records the receipt atomically; a repeated call with the same key and payload returns that receipt without another effect; a payload mismatch is rejected. Atomic serialization implies at most one effect for k: only the first absent-to-present transition can create it. If no effect has occurred, a delivered call can create it; if it has occurred, a delivered retry returns its receipt. Under eventual successful delivery and service progress, retrying the same stored key therefore yields exactly one effect and a receipt. This is a conditional sufficiency argument, not a claim that existing tools implement this contract.

reasoning_steps.title: State the remaining boundaries of that contract
reasoning_steps.argument: The contract fails to establish exactly-once behavior if recovery generates a fresh key, keys collide across logical operations, records expire before retries, or recording the receipt and performing the effect are separate crashable operations. For example, committing an effect and then crashing before recording M[k] recreates the original ambiguity. Eventual delivery gives eventual completion, not a finite-H guarantee. Per-operation deduplication also does not prove that the payload was correct, that a multi-service workflow is atomic, or that delayed external consequences are harmless.

reasoning_steps.title: Specify a falsifiable fault-injection test
reasoning_steps.argument: Use a synthetic append service with a hidden audit ledger as the ground-truth oracle. Fork identical pending checkpoints into W0 and W1. Compare always-retry, checkpoint restart without deduplication, safe escalation, and stable-key retry against an atomic deduplicating service. Include normal acknowledgment and permanently unavailable-service controls. Fix task payloads, model/prompt/tool versions, retry limits, H, and total budgets; randomize policy assignment and execution order across isolated task instances. Audit effect counts, terminal-report truth, unrelated-state changes, time to detection, escalation, calls, latency, and cost. The discriminating outcome is duplication in W1 or omission in W0 for local-only recovery, versus one effect after delivered stable-key retries under the specified contract. A policy apparently exceeding the bound requires inspecting whether it received distinguishing information or violated another construction assumption. Treat paired histories from one task as a cluster, retain all attempted runs, and report oracle-unavailable runs conservatively as uncertified rather than dropping them. Repeat across independent tasks and prespecified seeds; larger samples assess variability, not the universal theorem. This experiment is proposed, not executed.

output.claim: A stratified, paired architectural comparison can support a conservative improvement claim despite correlated judge errors and arbitrary dependence among repeated runs of a task. Here D_obs is the weighted task-cluster average of conservative certification differences, η_Ah bounds false certification by the intervention's judge, and ξ_Bh bounds missed true successes for the baseline. L>0 certifies positive improvement at the stated confidence level only if these truth-error allowances are justified. This is an analytical evaluation result, not evidence that any architectural mechanism improves agents.
output.method: Develop a standalone paired-comparison guarantee and specify its use in a controlled test of retry idempotency. Hypothesis: an idempotency mechanism improves true fixed-budget task success under ambiguous tool timeouts, rather than merely improving reported completion. The discriminating outcome is a positive lower bound L in prespecified timeout strata, accompanied by acceptable delayed-harm and cost measurements; failure to obtain L>0 is inconclusive, not proof of no benefit. Use identical task snapshots, model and prompt versions, tool capabilities, and hard resource limits; change only idempotency handling, account for its overhead, and isolate executions. The mathematical result assumes independent task clusters, prespecified population weights, and explicit directional judge-error allowances. No experiment was run because both supplied runtimes are unavailable. The supplied extract of artifact 0310e2ff-4aa0-4c95-b1a8-795559e484b8 motivates the oracle-error and task-clustering issues, but its original and truncated portions were not inspected; the proof here does not depend on their validity. reasoning_steps.title: Define the population, pairing, and estimand
reasoning_steps.argument: Choose finitely many strata h=1,...,H, with fixed target-population weights w_h≥0 summing to one. In each positive-weight stratum sample n_h≥1 independent task clusters. For each task, execute systems A and B in isolated copies of the same initial environment, using a fixed number r_h≥1 of scheduled runs per system. Within-cluster run dependence and dependence between systems are unrestricted. Let Y_shij be actual binary rubric satisfaction and S_shij=O_shij R_shij be joint automated acceptance and reference certification, for system s, cluster i, and run j. Define p_sh as the expectation of the cluster-average Y and p_s=Σ_h w_h p_sh. Thus the target is a weighted task distribution followed by uniform selection among scheduled runs, not a run-count-weighted mixture of tasks.

reasoning_steps.title: State the asymmetric truth-error allowances
reasoning_steps.argument: For a uniformly selected scheduled run in stratum h, assume Pr(S_A=1,Y_A=0)≤η_Ah and Pr(S_B=0,Y_B=1)≤ξ_Bh, with allowances in [0,1]. These are unconditional probabilities, not error rates conditional on certification. They need not be independent of agent behavior, each other, or task difficulty. The first controls intervention false certification; the second controls baseline true successes missed by certification. The earlier supplied extract discusses only a lower-bound-oriented allowance. The baseline missed-success allowance is an additional premise needed for this comparison, not something inferred from judge agreement.

reasoning_steps.title: Derive the population improvement inequality
reasoning_steps.argument: For binary Y and S, Y=S−1{S=1,Y=0}+1{S=0,Y=1}. Consequently E[Y_A]≥E[S_A]−η_Ah and E[Y_B]≤E[S_B]+ξ_Bh in stratum h. Subtracting the second inequality from the first gives Δ_h≥E[S_A−S_B]−η_Ah−ξ_Bh. Multiplying by nonnegative weights and summing yields Δ≥d−E_err, where d=Σ_h w_h E[S_A−S_B] and E_err=Σ_h w_h(η_Ah+ξ_Bh). Also Δ≥−1. No independence of the judges was used.

reasoning_steps.title: Explain why two reliability lower bounds cannot establish improvement
reasoning_steps.argument: Consider S_A=1 and S_B=0 on every execution, with Y_A=Y_B=1. Both systems have zero false certification. Their certification-based reliability lower bounds can be 1 and 0, yet their true improvement is zero, not one. Thus subtracting lower bounds can overstate improvement. In this example ξ_B=1, so the additional baseline allowance correctly removes the apparent improvement. This is an identification counterexample, not an observed agent result.

reasoning_steps.title: Concentrate independent task clusters rather than dependent runs
reasoning_steps.argument: Let X_hi=(1/r_h)Σ_j(S_Ahij−S_Bhij), so X_hi∈[−1,1], and D=Σ_h(w_h/n_h)Σ_i X_hi. Under independent clusters, E[D]=d. A centered variable supported on an interval of length 2 has moment-generating function at most exp(λ²/2). Applying this bound to the weighted independent X_hi gives E[exp(λ(D−d))]≤exp(λ²V/2), where V=Σ_h w_h²/n_h. Markov's inequality and minimization at λ=t/V give Pr(D−d≥t)≤exp(−t²/(2V)). Taking t=sqrt(2V log(1/α)) shows d≥D−t with probability at least 1−α. Repetition count r_h does not enter the worst-case radius: perfectly correlated repeats cannot create additional independent tasks.

reasoning_steps.title: Handle missing judgments conservatively without discarding tasks
reasoning_steps.argument: Define complete certification variables by the fixed judging protocol, whether or not each label is observed. For any missing S_A replace it by 0, and for any missing S_B replace it by 1; known labels remain unchanged. Let D_obs be the resulting weighted cluster difference. Pointwise D_obs≤D, even if missingness is outcome-dependent or correlated across tasks. Therefore the complete-data concentration event also implies d≥D_obs−t. This argument requires a well-defined complete protocol and scheduled denominators. It does not permit deleting missing tasks, silently treating missing truth labels as known, or applying complete-case analysis. A timeout is an actual failure only if the prespecified success rubric makes it one.

reasoning_steps.title: Combine the bounds and state coverage and edge cases
reasoning_steps.argument: On the event from the preceding steps, Δ≥D_obs−E_err−t and Δ≥−1, establishing the claimed L. For fixed valid allowances, coverage is at least 1−α. If allowances are instead simultaneous upper confidence bounds valid with probability at least 1−β, union bounding gives coverage at least 1−α−β, without requiring calibration and evaluation samples to be independent. Their statistical validity and target-population applicability still require justification. Zero-weight strata may be omitted; positive-weight unsampled strata are outside this theorem. With one cluster the bound remains valid but is usually uninformative. All missing labels give D_obs=−1 and hence L=−1. Multiple mechanisms, endpoints, or interim looks require additional prespecified error allocation; this fixed-comparison result does not cover unrestricted search.

reasoning_steps.argument: Proposed task family: multi-step ledger workflows requiring exactly one authorized transfer, correct recipient and amount, and a reconciled receipt after a fixed settlement horizon. reasoning_steps.argument: In the proposed controlled environment, evaluate actual terminal ledger state and receipt consistency rather than agent completion claims. An exhaustive outcome oracle would permit η_Ah=ξ_Bh=0 only after its coverage of the declared success predicate is justified; being a separate program is insufficient. reasoning_steps.title: 1. Replace only the invalid delivery-relaxation sentence
reasoning_steps.argument: Replace the last sentence of cycle 1, step 4 with: 'The displayed q-based bounds retain the retry-commitment premise of step 3. If issued retries may fail to commit, success in W0 still requires issuing a retry, but success in W1 need not require refraining from retry; therefore Pr(success|W1) <= 1-q is not established under that relaxation.' The supplied counterexample is decisive: always retry, drop every retry, and report completion. Then q=1, while W1 retains exactly one effect and the report can be true. This locally refutes the relaxed inequality, not the original proof. Keep the fair-coin tightness example restricted to external-effect correctness when its chosen retry commits exactly once; it does not establish the same tightness for independently certified completion.

reasoning_steps.title: 2. Preserve the core theorem with its original scope
reasoning_steps.argument: No change is needed to cycle 1, steps 1–3: in observationally identical W0 and W1, hidden-state-independent policy randomness gives the same probability q of issuing a first retry. When every issued retry commits before H and effects are irreversible, W0 success implies retry and W1 success implies no retry, so their success probabilities are bounded by q and 1-q. The worst-case failure bound of at least 1/2 consequently remains conditional on those premises. Without assured delivery, let N_i count additional committed effects by H in W_i. External-state correctness is exactly the event N_0=1 in W0 and N_1=0 in W1. No equality of the laws of N_0 and N_1 follows merely from identical information before the first retry. I therefore make no replacement delivery-relaxed probability theorem.

reasoning_steps.title: 3. Define the crash model and outcomes for the table
reasoning_steps.argument: Analyze one logical operation with fixed payload x. For a key k, write (c_k,r_k), where c_k is its number of irreversible committed effects and r_k is 1 iff a durable purported completion receipt exists. Let C=sum_k c_k count effects for the logical operation across all its keys. Initially all counts and receipt bits are zero. Attempts are serialized, including checking receipts, so the examples require no concurrency race. A receipt hit returns the stored receipt without performing another effect. A crash preserves completed durable transitions but discards the unfinished continuation; there is no background repair worker, separate effect-status query, or compensation. Stable recovery reuses the durably saved key and payload; regenerated recovery uses a previously unused key for the same logical operation. Keys do not collide, records do not expire, and payload mismatches are rejected. External-state correctness at H means C(H)=1. Full completion also requires a truthful terminal report. Eventual exactly-one completion means that after some finite time C remains one and truthful completion is reported, not merely that C transiently passes through one.

reasoning_steps.title: 4. Enumerate durable crash-boundary states
reasoning_steps.argument:
The following is an analytical transition table for a first, previously unseen key. A crash can occur at any displayed state; an atomic transition has no durable interior state.

| Implementation | Durable path on a receipt miss | Crash before first transition | Crash between transitions | Crash after both writes but before acknowledgment |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Atomic effect plus receipt | (0,0) -> (1,1) | (0,0) | Impossible under the contract | (1,1) |
| Effect before receipt | (0,0) -> (1,0) -> (1,1) | (0,0) | (1,0): effect exists, receipt absent | (1,1) |
| Receipt before effect | (0,0) -> (0,1) -> (1,1) | (0,0) | (0,1): receipt exists, effect absent | (1,1) |

A crash after acknowledgment but before the client durably saves completion leaves the same service states as the final column. In the receipt-before-effect row, 'receipt' deliberately denotes a record treated by this implementation as completed; an explicitly pending record with an independently correct recovery protocol is a different implementation. When effect and receipt involve different downstream systems, the atomic row applies only if the stipulated atomicity actually covers the external effect.

reasoning_steps.title: 5. Cross implementation with recovery-key policy
reasoning_steps.argument:
In this six-case table, 'clean retry' means a delivered retry that runs without another crash and whose response is delivered. Traces use the durable states from step 4; they are constructed possibilities, not observations.

| Service / key policy | Before either write | Interior crash boundary | After effect and receipt, acknowledgment lost | Consequence under continued recovery |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Atomic / stable | (0,0); retry k commits (1,1) | No such durable boundary | (1,1); retry k returns receipt, C stays 1 | At-most-one invariant always; a clean retry resolves either surviving state |
| Atomic / regenerated | Fresh k' can cleanly create the first effect if the old attempt never committed | No such durable boundary | k has (1,1); retry k' commits (1,1), so C=2 | Per-key uniqueness survives, logical-operation uniqueness does not |
| Effect-before-receipt / stable | Retry k can complete normally | k=(1,0); retry misses receipt, performs another effect, then writes receipt: (2,1) | k=(1,1); retry returns receipt without another effect | One gap crash followed by a clean retry duplicates; later progress does not remove it |
| Effect-before-receipt / regenerated | Fresh k' can complete normally if no old effect exists | k=(1,0); clean retry k' creates another effect, so C=2 | k=(1,1); clean retry k' again makes C=2 | A fresh key bypasses both recorded and unrecorded prior effects |
| Receipt-before-effect / stable | Retry k can complete normally | k=(0,1); every retry returns the receipt, so C remains 0 | k=(1,1); retry returns receipt with C=1 | Gap crash causes permanent omission under this handler, even with perfect subsequent delivery |
| Receipt-before-effect / regenerated | Fresh k' can complete normally | k=(0,1); clean fresh-key retry can create one effect and repair this particular omission | k=(1,1); clean retry k' creates a second effect | Fresh keys repair one constructed gap history but duplicate the post-effect history; no general exactly-one guarantee |

For every row, if the first attempt crashes before any write and all further useful execution is delayed past H, C(H)=0. That is a deadline omission even in the atomic/stable case, not a violation of its at-most-one safety invariant.

reasoning_steps.title: 6. Prove the atomic/stable invariant and its liveness boundary
reasoning_steps.argument: For atomic/stable recovery, induction over serialized service transitions proves (c_k,r_k) is always either (0,0) or (1,1). The base case is (0,0). A receipt miss makes the single atomic transition to (1,1); a receipt hit leaves that state unchanged; a crash preserves one of those states. All attempts use k, so C=c_k<=1. Thus a receipt cannot falsely certify a missing effect, and a lost acknowledgment cannot cause duplication. If recovery eventually has a surviving delivered call and returns its response, that call either creates the unique effect or retrieves its existing receipt, establishing eventual effect-and-receipt completion. A client that then persists completion and reports truthfully can finish. Infinite crashes, permanently lost responses, or exhausted retry budgets defeat that liveness premise without defeating the safety invariant.

reasoning_steps.title: 7. Explain why weaker invariants fail
reasoning_steps.argument: Atomic recording with fresh keys proves c_k<=1 separately for each k, but it does not bound sum_k c_k by one. Effect-before-receipt lacks the implication 'effect exists => receipt exists'; the gap permits an already committed action to be re-executed. Receipt-before-effect lacks the reverse implication 'receipt exists => effect exists'; the gap suppresses work that never happened and can produce a false completion report. These are distinct failure-propagation paths: ambiguity -> retry -> duplication versus premature certification -> suppressed retry -> omission. A receipt-before-effect intent log with a correct pending/completed distinction and reconciliation is outside the table's suppress-on-hit semantics, not refuted by this local omission trace. Likewise, effect-side deduplication would change the effect-before-receipt model.

reasoning_steps.title: 8. Separate eventual progress, deadline completion, and delayed duplication
reasoning_steps.argument: Eventual successful delivery supplies no fixed-H guarantee: an otherwise successful execution can have its first useful call or response delayed until H+1. As one sufficient stronger condition for atomic/stable recovery, suppose recovery starts at t0, faults cease by t0+B, the next retry is sent within delta, its full service interaction and response take at most S, and durable client completion plus truthful reporting take at most A. If t0+B+delta+S+A<=H, completion by H follows from step 6. These are hard conditional bounds, not measured latencies. For the other five cases, finite faults followed by clean progress still admit the table's persistent omission or duplication traces; progress alone cannot repair their safety/certification defects. Moreover C(H)=1 is only a horizon-specific count: a regenerated-key retry after H can create delayed duplication. A deadline experiment must separately specify whether outstanding or future actions are canceled and audit a later settlement horizon. Atomic/stable safety covers later same-key retries as long as retention and key identity persist.

reasoning_steps.title: 9. Specify the next discriminating test and retain evidential limits
reasoning_steps.argument: The next executable test should implement the 3-by-2 table in an isolated append service with an independent effect ledger. Inject a single crash before the first write, in each available interior gap, and after both writes with the acknowledgment withheld; separately crash the client before completion persistence. Follow with a clean retry, then repeat under permanent outage, delayed response beyond H, and an additional late retry. Audit C at H and a prespecified settlement horizon, receipt truth, client reports, recovery calls, latency, and cost. Include no-fault controls and matched payloads, retry schedules, budgets, and H across arms; retain every attempted run. Deterministic boundary coverage should precede seeded stochastic schedules and independent task-cluster repetitions. Discriminators are C=2 for effect-before-receipt/stable and post-commit regenerated-key traces, C=0 with a receipt for receipt-before-effect/stable, and only (0,0)/(1,1) for atomic/stable.
